title: Research Bite #8: Professional Development & Cognitive Load
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #8 covers Arielle Boguslav, Josh Goodrich, and Ollie Lovell's “Professional Development & Cognitive Load,” which applies cognitive load theory not to students but to teachers themselves as they try to implement new instructional strategies. The paper's central argument is that teacher coaching and CPD frequently fail not because the strategies being taught are wrong, but because attempting them in the live, high-stakes environment of a classroom overloads a teacher's own working memory — simultaneously managing behavior, content, and a brand-new technique is often simply too much at once. The authors offer a practical toolkit for coaches and CPD designers organized around reducing that load: chunking complex skills into rehearsable pieces, building routines and systems that remove in-the-moment decisions, planning solutions to recurring problem-spots in advance, narrowing what a teacher needs to attend to in high-load moments (like the first fifteen minutes of a lesson), using external cues and reminders rather than relying on memory, and even deliberately delaying non-urgent responses until cognitive load is lower. Barton's implication for anyone designing or receiving CPD is a reframe: effective coaching often starts by taking something away from a teacher's plate, not adding a new strategy on top of an already full one.
points: The paper's core reframe of teacher CPD is genuinely load-bearing: coaching often needs to remove cognitive demands from a teacher's plate before it can successfully add a new strategy, not simply layer the new strategy on top.

Chunking and automating — rehearsing a new strategy in simplified contexts, or focusing on just one new skill at a time — treats a teacher's own skill acquisition with the same cognitive-load logic normally applied to students learning content.

Systematization (routines, timers, seating charts, pre-gathered materials) works by eliminating in-the-moment decisions entirely, freeing scarce working memory for the actual new strategy a teacher is trying to embed.

Narrowing and re-focusing attention during known high-load periods — the authors specifically flag the first fifteen minutes of a lesson — gives coaches a concrete, time-bound target for where to concentrate support.

Managing emotion is treated as a legitimate cognitive-load lever, not a soft add-on: reframing stress, mindfulness, and validation are positioned alongside chunking and systematization as core CPD strategies.
quotes: Professional Development & Cognitive Load,” explores the challenges of cognitive load in teacher development. It presents a framework for understanding the impact of cognitive load on teachers in the classroom, including how it can hinder their ability to implement new teaching strategies and manage student behaviour.

Break down complex tasks into smaller, manageable chunks that can be automated through rehearsal and practice. Examples include rehearsing in simplified contexts, focusing on one new skill at a time, assigning student roles, using seating charts, and practising repeatedly.

Establish common routines and systems to manage classroom activities, minimizing the need for in-the-moment decisions. This includes using timers or cues, organizing tools, and gathering materials in advance.

Help teachers prioritize essential information and ignore less important distractions, particularly during high cognitive load periods. This can involve managing the first 15 minutes of class, pointing out important cues, and providing explicit guidance on what to focus on.

Encourage teachers to defer addressing non-urgent student behaviour or questions until periods of lower cognitive load. Techniques include note-taking, developing “breathing systems” to gain processing time and pre-setting rules for specific lesson segments.

Because of the high cognitive load involved in teaching, helping teachers to become more effective in the classroom often initially requires not adding, but taking away: finding ways to help teachers free up cognitive resources - or stop doing something - so that they can focus on what matters.
